questions.question: A test is 99% sensitive and 95% specific. The disease affects 1% of people. You test positive. Which is closest to your chance of being sick?
questions.explanation: Out of 10,000 people: 99 true positives and 495 false positives. Only 99 of the 594 positives are really sick, about 16.7%. The low base rate dominates.

questions.question: Which quantity do you usually want from a medical test?
questions.explanation: A patient who has tested positive wants to know the probability they are sick, P(sick | positive). The test's published accuracy is the reverse, P(positive | sick).

questions.question: In the 10,000-person table, how many people test positive in total?
questions.explanation: 99 true positives + 495 false positives = 594. This total is the denominator of the posterior.

questions.question: Keeping the same test, the disease rate rises from 1% to 30%. What happens to P(sick | positive)?
questions.explanation: A higher prior means far more true positives relative to false positives. With a 30% prior the posterior is about 89.5%. The same test means different things in different populations.

questions.question: 40% of emails are spam. 'FREE' appears in 80% of spam and 10% of real mail. What is P(spam | 'FREE')?
What is 'base-rate neglect'?
options: Ignoring how common something is and trusting the test's accuracy alone
questions.explanation: Base-rate neglect is treating P(positive | sick) as if it were P(sick | positive), forgetting the prior. It leads to wildly overconfident conclusions from a single positive result.
